question: What is the main chemical messenger the endocrine system uses to send signals around the body?
explanation: Think of hormones as the body's internal mail system! Endocrine glands release them straight into the bloodstream to tell different organs what to do. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h1)

question: Why does the body need to control hormone release very carefully?

options.A: To keep blood volume extremely high at all times
options.B: To replace lost nerve impulses during physical stress
options.C: To ensure the kidneys filter blood at a constant rate
options.D: To prevent chaos in the body and keep things stable

explanation: Too much or too little of a hormone can upset your body's balance (homeostasis). Careful control keeps everything running smoothly! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h1)

question: When an endocrine gland responds to 'humoral' stimulation, what is it actually reacting to?

options.A: Direct commands from the cerebral cortex
options.B: Levels of nutrients and ions in the blood
options.C: Electrical signals from the spinal cord
options.D: The presence of circulating releasing factors

explanation: Great job remembering this! 'Humoral' just means the gland is tasting the blood for things like calcium or glucose and reacting to what it finds. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h2)

question: A patient eats a heavy carbohydrate meal, and their blood sugar goes up. What happens next?

options.A: The pituitary gland secretes growth hormone
options.B: The pancreas secretes insulin to lower blood sugar
options.C: The parathyroid glands release parathyroid hormone
options.D: The adrenal cortex stops producing aldosterone

explanation: You see this every day! High blood sugar acts as a signal to the pancreas, telling it to release insulin to bring your glucose back to normal. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h2)

question: Which gland is directly stimulated by the nervous system when you are stressed or scared?
explanation: When your fight-or-flight response kicks in, nerves directly zap the adrenal medulla to pump out adrenaline instantly! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h3)

question: How does neural control of hormones differ from humoral control?

options.A: Neural control takes hours to respond compared to fast humoral pathways
options.B: Neural control relies entirely on negative feedback loops in the liver
options.C: Neural control uses direct nerve impulses rather than blood metabolite monitoring
options.D: Neural control only regulates reproductive organs instead of metabolic ones

explanation: Neural means nerves sending direct electrical messages, while humoral means the gland is checking chemicals floating in the blood. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h3)

question: What exactly is a 'tropic' hormone?

options.A: A hormone whose primary target is another endocrine gland
options.B: A neurotransmitter that acts locally inside the brain tissue
options.C: A hormone that is released directly in response to blood calcium
options.D: An enzyme produced by the liver to break down circulating fats

explanation: Think of tropic hormones as boss hormones—their job is to travel to other glands and tell them to release their own hormones! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h4)

question: Why is having a chain of command (hierarchical system) for hormones helpful for the body?

options.A: It prevents any possibility of hormone overproduction or toxicity
options.B: It allows a central brain region to coordinate widespread body responses
options.C: It eliminates the need for negative feedback loops in peripheral organs
options.D: It ensures that blood glucose levels remain entirely independent of brain activity

explanation: Having the brain act as the head office allows it to smoothly manage and coordinate multiple glands all over the body at once. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h4)

question: What is the main job of a negative feedback loop in the endocrine system?

options.A: To destroy excess neurotransmitters in synapses
options.B: To prevent hormone levels from rising too high
options.C: To amplify initial chemical signals rapidly
options.D: To stimulate continuous runaway glandular growth

explanation: Negative feedback is like a thermostat: when things get high enough, it tells the system to turn down the heat and restore balance. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h5)

question: If thyroid hormone levels in the blood get very high, what happens to thyroid-stimulating hormone (TSH) from the pituitary?

options.B: TSH release decreases due to negative feedback
options.C: TSH release stops entirely and permanently
options.D: TSH release increases to match thyroid hormone levels

explanation: When there is already plenty of thyroid hormone around, the pituitary gets the memo and slows down its TSH output so you don't overheat! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h5)

question: How does a positive feedback loop work in the body?

options.A: It stops hormone production the moment a target organ is reached
options.B: It constantly brings a fluctuating variable back to an exact baseline
options.C: It uses neural impulses exclusively to monitor blood calcium levels
options.D: It amplifies or intensifies a physiological change until an event finishes

explanation: Unlike negative feedback, positive feedback pushes a process harder and faster until a specific big event is done—like childbirth! [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h6)

question: Why is positive feedback much less common in the human body than negative feedback?

options.A: Positive feedback prevents endocrine glands from ever storing synthesized hormones
options.B: Positive feedback requires nervous system input, which is too slow for everyday metabolism
options.C: Positive feedback only functions when a person is resting and never during exercise
options.D: Positive feedback pushes systems away from normal balance and can cause harm if unchecked

explanation: Because positive feedback snowballs a change rather than calming it down, using it all the time would be dangerous for everyday stability. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h6)

question: Which part of the brain acts as the direct link between the nervous system and the endocrine system?
explanation: The hypothalamus is the master bridge! It takes nervous system signals and translates them into hormonal commands for the pituitary gland. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h7)

question: What is the main job of the anterior pituitary gland in the neuroendocrine system?

options.A: It generates electrical impulses for sympathetic flight responses
options.B: It monitors blood glucose levels via direct humoral sensation
options.C: It releases tropic hormones in response to hypothalamic signals
options.D: It stores oxytocin and antidiuretic hormone produced by neurons

explanation: The anterior pituitary takes messages from the hypothalamus and releases its own hormones to control other glands in the body. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h7)

question: What are the two main categories of hormone disorders?
explanation: Keep it simple: hormone problems usually happen because the body makes either too much (excess) or too little (deficiency) of a hormone. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h8)

question: A patient has signs of hormone overproduction because their feedback loop broke. What is the most likely cause?

options.A: Blood metabolite levels have successfully stabilized all endocrine organs
options.B: The target gland or pituitary fails to respond to negative feedback inhibition
options.C: The hypothalamus stops releasing releasing factors entirely and permanently
options.D: Neural stimulation of the adrenal medulla has permanently shut down

explanation: If the 'off switch' (negative feedback) stops working, the gland keeps pumping out hormones without stopping, leading to overproduction. [learn more](GNS211_U1_T6#GNS211_U1_T6_h8)
